::: {.callout-note}
## What this page is about

A collected set of practical tips for running OpenFOAM well, aimed at the course
**project** (design, verify and validate a RANS case). None of it is new physics;
it is the kind of hard-won, rule-of-thumb advice that saves you days of wasted
compute. Treat it as a reference you come back to, not a recipe to follow blindly:
every case is different, so understand *why* each tip works before you apply it.
If you have not run a case yet, start with the
[OpenFOAM how-to](how-to.qmd) and come back here once you are setting up your own
geometry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The one rule to remember
**Good mesh, good results. Garbage in, garbage out.** Most OpenFOAM pain, divergence,
smeared gradients, wrong forces, traces back to a poor mesh or a boundary condition
that does not represent the physics. Spend your time there first. And when you run:
**start robustly, end accurately** — begin with stable, low-order settings and tighten
toward accuracy as the solution settles.
:::

## The workflow, and where the effort goes

Every case follows the same path, and the earlier a mistake enters it, the more
expensive it is to fix:

```text
geometry  →  mesh  →  case set-up (0/, constant/, system/)  →  solve  →  post-process
```

Aim for a **clean, watertight geometry**, then a **good-quality mesh**, before you
touch schemes or turbulence models. A beautiful discretization scheme cannot rescue
a bad mesh, and no amount of post-processing can rescue an unconverged run.

## Finding your way around OpenFOAM

The installation ships with its own documentation: thousands of working tutorial
cases and the full source code. Learn to search them, and you rarely need anything
else.

```bash
echo $FOAM_TUTORIALS   # ready-to-run example cases — your best templates
echo $FOAM_SRC         # the library source code
echo $FOAM_SOLVERS     # the solver applications
```

```bash
# find a case that uses a given boundary condition, keyword or solver:
find $FOAM_TUTORIALS -type f | xargs grep -sl 'limitedLinear'

# locate the source file behind a keyword (e.g. a BC or scheme):
find $FOAM_SRC -iname '*slip*'

# list every dictionary file ending in "Dict" in the tutorials:
find $FOAM_TUTORIALS -iname '*Dict'
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The "banana" trick
OpenFOAM keyword wrong or unsure of the options? Put a deliberately invalid value
(the community favourite is `banana`) and run the application. It stops and prints
**the full list of valid entries** for that keyword:

```bash
# in system/fvSchemes, set:  div(phi,U)  Gauss banana;
simpleFoam
# -> error message lists every available div scheme
```
:::

The single best way to set up a new case is to **copy the closest tutorial case** and
modify it, rather than writing dictionaries from scratch.

## Keep a tidy case (it matters on clusters)

- **No spaces or special characters** in file, directory or variable names, and do
  not start a name with an underscore. Use `my_case`, not `my case!` or `_my_case`.
  Funny characters break scripts, especially on clusters.
- Keep the case self-contained and scripted. Most tutorials ship an `Allrun` and
  `Allclean` script — use the same pattern so a grader (or future-you) can
  reproduce the result with one command. This is exactly the **reproducibility**
  the project asks for.
- Always pipe the solver output to a log so you can plot residuals later:

```bash
simpleFoam | tee log.simpleFoam
foamCleanTutorials        # or ./Allclean — reset the case to its initial state
```

## Mesh quality and `checkMesh`

For how `blockMesh` and `snappyHexMesh` actually build a mesh, see the
[meshing overview](meshing.qmd). Whichever you use, check it before you run. Always.

```bash
blockMesh        # or your meshing tool / snappyHexMesh
checkMesh        # should end with "Mesh OK."
```

`checkMesh` reports the metrics that control accuracy and stability, and flags
topological errors (which you *must* fix). Watch especially:

| Metric | What to watch for | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| non-orthogonality | max should be well below 70° | controls the Laplacian scheme and corrections |
| skewness | keep low (< ~4) | smears gradients, hurts accuracy |
| aspect ratio | moderate, except in the boundary layer | very high AR slows the solver |
| $y^+$ | consistent with your wall treatment | wall-resolved $y^+\!\lesssim\!1$ vs. wall-function $30\!\lesssim\!y^+\!\lesssim\!300$ |

::: {.callout-warning}
## A mesh that "runs" is not a mesh that is right
OpenFOAM will often run on a poor mesh, but skewness, high aspect ratio and
non-orthogonality **silently degrade accuracy** and can make the solver crawl or
diverge. If `checkMesh` complains, fix the mesh — usually that means remeshing.
To *see* the offending cells, convert the failed sets and open them in ParaView:

```bash
checkMesh            # writes faulty cells/faces to constant/polyMesh/sets/
foamToVTK -faceSet skewFaces   # (or the set name checkMesh reported)
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Renumber for speed
On larger meshes, run `renumberMesh -overwrite` after meshing. It reorders the cells
to reduce the matrix bandwidth, which makes the linear solver faster — a free speed-up.
:::

## Boundary and initial conditions

- **They must be physically realistic.** For every field you solve you need a
  boundary condition on every patch (and a sensible initial field).
- **Put boundaries far from the action.** Keep inlets and outlets away from
  separation, recirculation and strong gradients so they do not contaminate the
  solution; this also feeds the domain-independence argument in your report.
- **Do not over-specify the outlet.** Use `zeroGradient` (or an
  `inletOutlet`/`pressureOutlet`-type condition) so the solver extrapolates the
  flow leaving the domain; forcing values there causes trouble. Watch for
  **back-flow** at outlets.
- **Good initial conditions speed convergence.** A `potentialFoam` solution, a
  solution mapped from a coarse mesh (`mapFields`), or a converged laminar/steady
  field all make a good starting point. Unphysical starts slow convergence or
  cause divergence.

## Running the solver: start robust, end accurate

- **Change settings on the fly.** Set `runTimeModifiable yes;` in `controlDict` and
  you can edit `fvSchemes`, `fvSolution` and `controlDict` while the solver runs.
- **Ramp toward accuracy.** Begin with a robust, low-order configuration (e.g.
  `upwind`, loose linear-solver tolerances, heavier under-relaxation), then switch to
  a second-order scheme and tighten tolerances once the solution stabilises. If it
  starts to oscillate, drop back to upwind, let it settle, and climb again.
- **Monitor a quantity of interest, not just residuals.** Residuals falling is
  necessary but not sufficient. Add a `solverInfo` function object for the residual
  history, and monitor your QoI (a force coefficient, a reattachment length, a
  pressure drop) until it levels off — that is your real convergence criterion, and
  the one the project asks you to report.
- **Watch the continuity errors.** The per-step `time step continuity errors` should
  stay small; if they grow, something is wrong (mesh, BCs, or time step).

```{.cpp filename="system/fvSolution (SIMPLE)"}
SIMPLE
{
    nNonOrthogonalCorrectors 1;      // raise to 1–2 on non-orthogonal meshes
    consistent      yes;
    residualControl { p 1e-4; U 1e-4; "(k|epsilon|omega)" 1e-4; }
}
relaxationFactors
{
    equations { U 0.7; "(k|epsilon|omega)" 0.7; }
    fields    { p 0.3; }             // pressure is under-relaxed the most
}
```

## Discretization schemes (`fvSchemes`)

### Convective terms — `divSchemes`

Pick by the stability/accuracy trade-off; these are the ones you will actually use:

| Scheme | Order / behaviour | When |
|---|---|---|
| `upwind` | 1st order, very stable, diffusive | to start a run, or to stabilise a blow-up |
| `linearUpwind grad(U)` | 2nd order, bounded | a good default for momentum |
| `limitedLinear 1` | 2nd order, TVD, bounded | the turbulence scalars $k$, $\varepsilon$, $\omega$ (keeps them positive) |
| `vanLeer` / `Minmod` | 2nd order, TVD, bounded | scalars where you want a classic limiter |
| `linear` | 2nd order, unbounded | smooth fields on good meshes; can oscillate |

::: {.callout-important}
## Never submit a final result computed with first-order schemes
First-order upwind is for *starting* and *stabilising* only — it is too diffusive, it
smears gradients and under-predicts forces. Your reported, validated result must use a
second-order scheme. (This is also why the verification study matters: mesh refinement
and scheme order together set your numerical uncertainty.)
:::

### Diffusive terms — `laplacianSchemes` and non-orthogonality

The Laplacian (and surface-normal gradient) scheme is tied directly to mesh
non-orthogonality through a blending factor $\psi$ in `Gauss linear limited ψ`:

| Max non-orthogonality | Scheme | Blending $\psi$ |
|---|---|---|
| low (< 70°) | `Gauss linear corrected` | full correction (most accurate) |
| moderate (70–85°) | `Gauss linear limited 0.5` | $\psi = 0.5$ (stable compromise) |
| high (> 85°) | `Gauss linear limited 0.333` | low $\psi$ + more `nNonOrthogonalCorrectors` — or remesh |

$\psi = 1$ keeps full accuracy on a good mesh; lowering $\psi$ trades accuracy for
stability on a poor one. The right answer is almost always a better mesh.

### Gradient terms — `gradSchemes`

`Gauss linear` is the robust default; `leastSquares` is more accurate but can be
oscillatory on tetrahedral meshes. Both are second order.

## Running on the cluster and heavy I/O

- **Save in binary.** Set `writeFormat binary;` in `controlDict` for faster, smaller
  output — a real difference on big cases. (See the [cluster](../cluster/index.qmd)
  pages for Slurm, modules and parallel runs with `decomposePar`/`mpirun`.)
- **Do not write too often.** I/O is frequently the bottleneck and can fill your
  scratch quota; pick a sensible `writeInterval`, but make sure you write *before*
  the job hits its time limit.
- **Double-check your job script before you queue.** A two-day wait followed by a
  typo'd script that never starts is the most common cluster time-sink.

## When it blows up: a quick checklist

::: {.callout-warning}
## Divergence / "floating point exception" — work through this list
1. **Check the mesh** (`checkMesh`): fix topological errors, reduce skewness/non-orthogonality.
2. **Drop to first order** (`upwind`) and loosen tolerances to get *a* solution, then climb back up.
3. **Under-relax more** (steady) or **cut the time step / Courant number** (transient).
4. **Re-read the boundary conditions** — a wrong inlet/outlet or missing wall function is a classic cause.
5. **Raise `nNonOrthogonalCorrectors`** if the mesh is non-orthogonal.
6. **Start from a better initial field** (`potentialFoam`, or map a coarse solution).

Change one thing at a time so you learn what actually fixed it.
:::
